analysis.one_liner: Shields gun and ammunition makers and sellers from most lawsuits over harm caused by criminal misuse of their products.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Commerce Committee at the end of the 107th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal law to bar courts from imposing civil damages or other penalties on gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and their trade associations for harm caused when someone else criminally misuses a firearm. It lists firearms companies with the Commerce Department and declares their lawful conduct — making, selling, or promoting guns — immune from lawsuits or court orders stemming from gun crimes committed by other people. Narrow exceptions are preserved for defective products and contract or warranty claims. The bill never advanced past referral to the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations would gain near-immunity from civil suits arising from the criminal misuse of their products. Today, victims of shootings and cities sue the industry over how it markets and distributes guns; this bill would end those suits, shifting the costs of gun violence from the industry to victims, families, and public health systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun makers, sellers, and their trade groups

how_it_helps.text: It would bar federal, state, and local courts from awarding civil damages or other relief against firearms and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, or their trade associations for harms caused when someone else criminally misuses a gun.
It would shield not only the companies but their trade associations from suits, and would cover any lawful conduct by a licensed manufacturer or seller in placing a firearm in the stream of commerce.
It preserves only narrow exceptions: breach of contract or warranty, and injuries caused directly by a defective product when used as intended.

analysis.who_pays: Victims of gun violence and their families would bear the cost: they would lose the ability to sue manufacturers, sellers, or trade associations over the industry's marketing and distribution practices, even under state law. Cities and states would likewise lose a tool they have used to recover the public costs of gun violence.
analysis.who_pays_short: Victims of gun violence and their families

drawbacks.text: It would strip victims of gun crimes of the ability to sue manufacturers, dealers, or trade associations over how firearms were marketed, distributed, or sold into the stream of commerce, even under state law claims.

The protection covers trade associations as well as manufacturers and sellers, and applies to any conduct lawful under federal firearms law or state law, a bar that would apply nationwide regardless of state court rules on negligent selling or marketing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the industry, the benefit is decisive: it would end the main legal avenue — municipal and private lawsuits over marketing and distribution practices — for holding gun makers and sellers accountable for how their products reach criminals. For ordinary people, the cost is equally real: victims of gun violence and their families would lose the ability to sue the businesses whose sales practices put the weapon in the shooter's hands, even when state law would otherwise allow it. The bill reserves only narrow product-liability claims (a defective gun that fires when dropped), leaving the larger public-safety harms unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Introduced April 25, 2002 by Senator Zell Miller, with 46 cosponsors including 40 Senate Republicans and 6 Senate Democrats.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction; no markup, hearing, or floor vote followed.
The bill died at the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003, without ever receiving a committee or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun violence victims and municipalities suing the gun industry are better off, since their right to sue remained intact for the moment; the industry lost a shot at federal immunity, though a similar version became law in 2005.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun-violence victims' right to sue preserved

for.name: Sen. Zell Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 2268 to shield firearms manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations from lawsuits over criminal misuse of guns.

for.name: Sen. Larry Craig
for.what_they_did: Joined Miller in introducing the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican: 40 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored versus 6 of 49 Senate Democrats, under a Democratic sponsor from Georgia.

industries.note: The bill would give gun makers near-total immunity from civil lawsuits over harms caused by criminal misuse of their products, insulating them from the costs of litigation and potential damage awards. Lawful conduct in placing guns in commerce could no longer be the basis for any court-imposed restriction.
Sellers would be shielded alongside manufacturers from suits tied to how guns were distributed or sold, even where state law might treat a sale as negligent.

The bill explicitly protects trade associations representing manufacturers and sellers from suits over their representational and advisory activities, extending industry immunity to its lobbying and organizing arms.
The bill would eliminate the primary legal tool — product liability and negligence suits — used by victims and municipalities against the gun industry, eliminating an entire field of litigation.
